implementation_notes: slices.Clip is the standard library's named form: its whole implementation is s[:len(s):len(s)], a full slice expression that caps the returned header's capacity at its length, so no later append grows back into the tail of the old array and a reslice of the returned value cannot resurrect it. What it does not do is free anything: the backing array keeps its size and stays alive while any other slice of it exists, and the garbage collector releases an array only when it becomes unreachable. Use Clip when the intent is a bounded header - a defensive API boundary, or a guarantee that a later append copies rather than silently extending into memory the caller thinks was discarded - and reach for the rebuild variant when the bytes themselves must go back.
pitfalls: Clip caps the header only: the old array stays allocated and reachable through any other slice, reslice or cached subslice of it, so it is a bounds fix, not a release.
Clipping before the final append forces a reallocation: every append after Clip copies the elements, so apply it when growth has genuinely stopped.
A three-index expression s[:n:n] is the manual spelling of the same thing, and mixing it with a reslice whose capacity exceeds len silently re-opens the tail.
sources: Go standard library source, slices/slices.go (go1.22.0) - 'Clip removes unused capacity from the slice, returning s[:len(s):len(s)]', next to Clone ('Clone returns a copy of the slice. The elements are copied using assignment, so this is a shallow clone'): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/go1.22.0/src/slices/slices.go
Go 1.21 Release Notes - 'The new slices package provides many common operations on slices, using generic functions that work with slices of any element type': https://go.dev/doc/go1.21

variants.name: rebuild exactly (slices.Clone / append into an empty slice)
variants.implementation_notes: The form that actually returns memory: allocate a slice sized to the live range and copy the survivors into it - slices.Clone (Go 1.18, itself append(s[:0:0], s...)) or the pre-generics spelling with make + copy / append(s[:0:0], s...). The new array is as large as the live range and the old array becomes garbage as soon as nothing else references it; bytes.Clone and strings.Clone are the same operation for the standard buffers. Choose it when the peak allocation is the problem (large buffers held in long-lived structures); the price is one copy and a second allocation of the survivors' size, and any alias of the old slice keeps it alive.
pitfalls: A rebuild frees the old array only when every other slice of it is gone: subslices, reslices and cached headers keep it alive and keep writing into it.
The rebuild holds both buffers at once (transient 2x), and Clone copies only the elements - for a slice of pointers or structs holding buffers the peak stays alive one indirection down.
Go's garbage collector never shrinks an array in place, so a rebuild is the only release: three-index expressions and Clip bound the header without returning a byte.
